result: Cortical stress fibers are a distinct class of actomyosin bundles that are embedded in the ventral actin cortex, typically smaller than ventral stress fibers, and preferentially localize underneath or close to the nucleus at the rear of migrating cells.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C34, C35, C47, C59, and C60 collectively establish the spatial characteristics of cortical stress fibers through 3D-SIM imaging (Figure 1) and live-cell imaging (Figure 3A). The localization is well-documented with quantitative data showing ~80% assembly underneath the nucleus (C63, Figure 3B).

result: Cortical stress fibers share molecular composition with ventral stress fibers (bipolar NMII filaments, α-actinin, focal adhesion connections) but differ in key structural and functional properties: they are thinner, more dynamic, lack NMII stacks, have less regular α-actinin periodicity, and exert significantly weaker traction forces.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40, C45-C48, and C92-C98 are supported by multiple imaging modalities (3D-SIM in Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and quantitative traction force microscopy (Figure 1C, p=1.56×10⁻¹²). The molecular and structural characterization is comprehensive and internally consistent.

result: Cortical stress fibers assemble de novo from the ventral actin cortex through reorganization of cortical actin filaments into thicker bundles, followed by growth of vinculin-positive focal adhesions at both ends, without involvement of pre-existing stress fiber precursors.
evaluation: Claims C7, C49, C50, C51, and C89 are strongly supported by time-lapse TIRFM imaging (Figure 2A, 2B, Videos 1 and 2). The sequential assembly process is clearly documented, distinguishing this mechanism from the known transverse arc/dorsal stress fiber pathway for ventral stress fiber formation.

result: Unlike dorsal stress fibers, cortical stress fibers do not elongate through actin polymerization at focal adhesions, as demonstrated by photoactivation experiments showing nearly immobile photoactivated actin regions in cortical stress fibers versus centripetal movement (~0.3 µm/min) in dorsal stress fibers.
evaluation: Claims C52, C53, C54, and C97 are supported by photoactivation experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) with clear quantitative differences between cortical and dorsal stress fibers. The experimental design appropriately tests the hypothesis of actin polymerization-driven elongation.

result: Non-muscle myosin II pulses orchestrate cortical stress fiber assembly by driving reorganization of cortical actin meshwork into bundles. Most pulses are transient and non-productive, but persistent pulses lead to stable actomyosin bundles that engage and reinforce focal adhesions, promoting cortical stress fiber maturation.
evaluation: Claims C5, C8, C66-C70, C100, and C122 are supported by three-color TIRFM imaging (Figure 4A, Video 8) and kymograph analysis (Figure 4B, 4C). The distinction between productive and non-productive pulses is clearly demonstrated, and the temporal relationship between NMII pulses, actin bundling, and focal adhesion maturation is well-documented.

result: Cortical stress fiber assembly occurs preferentially underneath the nucleus during cell locomotion, with ~80% of cortical stress fibers assembling in this location despite the nucleus occupying <30% of cell area. NMIIA pulses are slightly more prevalent underneath the nucleus compared to regions outside the nucleus perimeter.
evaluation: Claims C62, C63, C64, and C65 are supported by quantitative analysis from 19 time-lapse videos (Figure 3B) and NMIIA pulse frequency measurements (Figure 3C, p=0.00012, paired t-test). The statistical analysis appropriately accounts for the area difference, strengthening the conclusion of preferential assembly.

result: NMII activity is critical for cortical stress fiber assembly, as demonstrated by near-complete abolition of cortical stress fiber formation in Blebbistatin-treated cells. Generation of cortical stress fibers is driven by NMII-catalyzed reorganization of the cortical actin filament network and is dependent on integrin-based cell-matrix adhesions.
evaluation: Claims C77, C78, C81, C87, and C88 are supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Video 11, Figure 4D) and experiments with cells lacking integrin-based adhesions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Video 12). The quantification shows clear differences between DMSO control and Blebbistatin treatment.

result: Focal adhesions associating with new cortical stress fibers can either emerge de novo or be pre-existing adhesions connected to other contractile bundles. Occasionally, one end of a cortical stress fiber connects to a mesh of pre-existing actomyosin bundles instead of a focal adhesion, demonstrating the dynamic and plastic nature of cortical stress fiber generation.
evaluation: Claims C71, C72, C73, and C74 are supported by time-lapse imaging (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B, Videos 9 and 10). The observations document multiple assembly pathways, though the relative frequency of each pathway is not quantified, which would strengthen the conclusions.

result: Cortical stress fibers are highly dynamic structures with a relatively short average half-life (~25 min), though individual half-lives vary widely from a few minutes to more than 1.5 hours. They often associate dynamically with each other and can arise via various intermediate assembly states.
evaluation: Claims C55, C56, C57, and C58 are supported by live-cell imaging experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Video 3). However, the manuscript does not provide detailed quantification of half-life measurements (sample size, measurement method), which limits full evaluation of the statistical robustness.

result: Blebbistatin does not cease myosin pulses in U2OS cells, indicating that myosin pulses do not depend on the catalytic activity of NMII but can occur when the motor domain is in a low actin-affinity state.
evaluation: Claims C75 and C76 are supported by imaging data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and a supporting citation (Baird et al., 2017). The interpretation that pulses are independent of catalytic activity is consistent with the mechanism of Blebbistatin action (Kovács et al., 2004).

result: Arp2/3 inhibition with CK-666 results in only a moderate decrease in cortical stress fiber numbers, with de novo assembly still frequently observed after 4 hours of treatment, indicating that Arp2/3 complex activity is not essential for cortical stress fiber formation.
evaluation: Claims C80 and C82 are supported by time-lapse imaging (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Video 13) and quantification (Figure 4D). The contrast with the near-complete loss following NMII inhibition strengthens the conclusion about the relative importance of these factors.

result: Treatment with the formin inhibitor SMIFH2 decreases cortical stress fiber numbers, suggesting formins contribute to their assembly. However, siRNA depletion of mDia1, mDia2, and mDia3 did not significantly reduce cortical stress fiber numbers, suggesting these formins are either not critical or are functionally redundant.
evaluation: Claims C83-C86 present conflicting results between SMIFH2 treatment (decreased cortical stress fibers) and siRNA experiments (no significant effect). The authors acknowledge this discrepancy and suggest functional redundancy, but this remains speculative. Additionally, SMIFH2 has known off-target effects on myosins (Nishimura et al., 2020), which complicates interpretation. Further experiments with combinatorial formin depletion would be needed to resolve this uncertainty.

result: Cortical stress fibers are most prevalently observed in cells migrating on fibronectin, though they can also form on laminin and collagen substrates.
evaluation: Claims C41 and C42 are supported by 3D-SIM imaging on different ECM substrates (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). However, the manuscript does not provide quantitative comparison of cortical stress fiber prevalence across different substrates, which would strengthen this conclusion.

result: Focal adhesions at the ends of cortical stress fibers contain Y118-phosphorylated paxillin, indicating they are not associated with fibrillar adhesions, which lack this phosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C43 and C44 are supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and are consistent with established markers distinguishing focal adhesions from fibrillar adhesions (Zaidel-Bar et al., 2007). The logic connecting Y118-p-paxillin presence to focal adhesion identity is sound.

result: U2OS cells migrating in 3D fibrin network exhibit short, adhesion-attached actomyosin bundles close to nuclei that may correspond to cortical stress fibers.
evaluation: Claim C121 is supported by imaging data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Video 6), but the authors explicitly state that whether these structures correspond to cortical stress fibers and are generated through the same mechanism remains an important question for future research. The 3D environment lacks the ventral/dorsal distinction present in 2D, making direct comparison challenging.

result: Transverse arc formation does not involve prominent myosin pulses but rather occurs through condensation of the lamellipodial actin filament network during the retraction phase, distinguishing it from cortical stress fiber assembly.
evaluation: Claims C90 and C91 are supported by citation to prior work (Burnette et al., 2011) and serve to contextualize the novelty of the cortical stress fiber assembly mechanism. This is established knowledge used for comparison rather than a new finding of this study.

result: NMII pulse-driven cortical actin condensations have been reported in epithelial tissues during development and in mesenchymal cells in 2D, where they drive tissue morphogenesis or undergo stabilization into other structures. This suggests myosin II pulse-driven F-actin bundling may have a general role in forming different types of contractile actomyosin bundles.
evaluation: Claims C102-C107 are supported by multiple citations to prior work and serve to place the current findings in broader context. Claim C105 and C107 represent speculation by the authors about general principles, which is appropriately qualified in the text.

result: The authors speculate that the de novo cortical stress fiber assembly mechanism may be particularly suited for generating stress fibers in 3D environments to protect the nucleus during migration through constrictions, where transverse arcs are not present and the nucleus faces mechanical challenges.
evaluation: Claims C113-C120 are primarily speculative discussion points supported by citations to prior work on nuclear mechanics and 3D migration. While the hypothesis is logical and well-motivated, it lacks direct experimental support in this manuscript. Claims C118 and C119 are explicitly speculative ('we envision', 'well suited'), and the connection to cortical stress fibers in 3D (C121) remains uncertain.

result: The introduction establishes background knowledge about actomyosin structures, including the actin cortex, stress fiber subtypes (ventral, dorsal, transverse arcs), their molecular composition, assembly mechanisms, and cellular functions.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C9-C33 represent established scientific knowledge supported by appropriate citations throughout the introduction. These claims provide necessary context for the novel findings but are not new results of this study.

result: The manuscript describes key methodological details including cell line authentication (U2OS from ATCC, verified by STR profiling), imaging systems (Deltavision OMX SR for 3D-SIM and TIRF), and experimental conditions (polyacrylamide gels with 26 kPa stiffness for traction force microscopy).
evaluation: Claims C124-C128 are methodological details stated in the Materials and Methods section. These are important for reproducibility and represent standard reporting practices. The cell line authentication and detailed imaging parameters support the rigor of the experimental approach.
